Human in the Loop Is Now Standard. Here Is What GCC Leaders Should Ask Next.

Finance software leaders now promise governed agents and human approvals. The sharper question for a GCC business is what the agent is allowed to act on.

By Lisa Warren · 26 November 2026

On this pageWhat changedThe gapVerified firstQuestions to askSources

AI governance in the GCC is moving from a policy paper to a purchasing question. When a vendor says its agents are governed and a human approves the important steps, how do you tell whether that is enough?

What changed this month

BlackLine first previewed its Finance Control Console in June and presented it again at BeyondTheBlack on 17 November. It describes the console as providing governance, policy enforcement and human-in-the-loop approvals for its AI agents. The same day it said it would bring governed agentic AI to the office of the CFO with OpenAI. In September, Trintech launched three more agents and said they work inside the controls, approvals and audit trails finance teams already use.

The message from the largest finance software vendors is consistent: agents act, people approve, and everything is logged. That is good news for buyers. It also means "a human is in the loop" no longer tells you much on its own.

The gap the label does not cover

An approval step governs what happens after an agent proposes something. It does not tell you whether the thing proposed rests on records that agree. In most businesses the orders, deliveries and invoices that feed an agent are written by different departments in different systems, and they disagree.

If an agent drafts an action from a record that conflicts with another team's record, the human approving it is being asked to resolve a disagreement the system never showed them.

Verified first, then a human decides

This is how we build Zonar OS and HALU. Zonar OS reconciles the records with rule-based, repeatable logic and ties every finding to a source row. HALU briefs the owner of each gap only from those verified findings. A person approves every action that matters, and every run and decision is logged. No evidence, no finding.

The order matters. Governance that starts at the approval step is checking the last link of the chain. Governance that starts with verification checks the first.

Five questions to ask any vendor of agentic AI

  1. What data does the agent act on, and who confirmed that data agrees across departments?
  2. Can every recommendation be traced to a source record?
  3. Which actions need a human approval, and who sets the limits?
  4. What is logged, and can your auditor read it?
  5. Where is the data held, and who in your region deploys and supports it?
